sentences.text: Purpose of this Part

paragraphs.text: (1) Within the context of rule 1.2, the purpose of this Part is (a) to obtain evidence that will be relied on in the action, (b) to narrow and define the issues between parties, (c) to encourage early disclosure of facts and records, (d) to facilitate evaluation of the parties' positions and, if possible, resolution of issues in dispute, and (e) to discourage conduct that unnecessarily or improperly delays proceedings or unnecessarily increases the cost of them. (2) The Court may give directions or make any order necessary to achieve the purpose of this Part.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 5.1:1 Rule 5.1 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.1. 1. The Alberta Discovery Regime See CNOOC Petroleum North America ULC v. 801 Seventh Inc., 2023 ABCA 97, 2023 CarswellAlta 674 (at paragraphs 20-33, and 35) for a broad overview of the discovery regime in Alberta. 2. Prolixity In 1400467 Alberta Ltd. v. Adderley, 2013 ABQB 656, 2013 CarswellAlta 2200, Madam Justice Veit said, at paragraphh 3: “This court has both the inherent and the explicit power to advance the objectives articulated in R. 5.1(1) by ordering the removal of prolix affidavits and requiring the filing of new affidavits.” Her Ladyship then said, at paragraphs 9–13: 9 Alberta's Rules do not specifically address prolixity or provide a remedy for prolixity where it exists. Indeed, the case law interpreting the rules relating to discovery of documents usually deals with a failure to provide adequate and timey disclose rather than with the problem caused by excessive, potentially irrelevant, disclosure. However, in Hill[Hill v. Hart-Davis (1884) 26 Ch. D. 470 (Eng. C.A.)], the English Court of Appeal long ago addressed this type of problem: Although there is no rule of court specially giving power to the Court to take pleadings or affidavits off the file for prolixity, yet the Court has an inherent power to do so in order to prevent its records from being made the instruments of oppression. (from the head-note). 10 Hill was a case in which 4,216 letters had been separately set out in the equivalent to an affidavit of records by their dates and names of the writers and recipients; in addition, a “vast number” of receipts had been disclosed. It was argued against the motion in that case that the court should not and could not, at that juncture, decide on the relevancy of the contested disclosure. If the equivalent of the affidavit of records was too long, then, it was argued, the appropriate remedy was to “inflict” costs. 11 In support of the unanimous decision that, on the facts of the particular case, only costs would be awarded although the Court did have the jurisdiction to remove the offending affidavit, one of the Law Lords said: I am not inclined to express any opinion whether the documents set out in the affidavit are relevant or not. But assuming that they are, it is perfectly plain to my mind that they might have been set out in a way which would not have been oppressive. There is a prolixity in this affidavit of which no account can be given except a desire to cause vexation and costs to the Defendant. 12 Dunn[Dunn v. Grass Systems (UK) Ltd.[2007] EWHC B2 (Q.B.)] is an example of a modern English decision which, even though it dealt with a much more serious matter which was the removal of a pleading rather than a mere affidavit, concluded that, in the circumstances, the only relief that was appropriate was the striking out of the pleading. 13 Alberta courts have the same inherent power as to English courts to ensure that purported compliance with the Rules of Court does not, in fact, become a technique for unnecessarily increasing the cost of litigation. In addition, Alberta courts have the explicit power to advance the objectives articulated in R. 5.1(1): R. 5.1(2). 3. Application to seek additional production In Questor Technology Inc v. Stagg, 2022 ABQB 578, 2022 CarswellAlta 2372, Justice D. B. Nixon commented on applications for additional record production. His Lordship said: [86] Where a party is found to be deliberately trying to thwart the discovery process by not disclosing relevant and material records, a court may make a more substantive production order: Innovative Health Group Inc v Calgary Health Region, 2008 ABCA 219 at para 39. The Rules permit this Court to make any order necessary to achieve the orderly disclosure of records: Rule 5.1(2). … [101] A party seeking additional production must provide a legal or factual foundation that additional relevant and material records exist: Parks at para 10. Court must be especially cognizant and vigilant when only one party has access to the records: Canadian Natural Resources Limited v ShawCor Ltd, 2013 ABQB 230 at para 19 [ShawCor]. [102] Where the evidence suggests that not all relevant and material records have been produced, a further and better affidavit of records may be ordered: ShawCor at para 19.

sentences.text: When something is relevant and material

paragraphs.text: (1) For the purposes of this Part, a question, record or information is relevant and material only if the answer to the question, or the record or information, could reasonably be expected (a) to significantly help determine one or more of the issues raised in the pleadings, or (b) to ascertain evidence that could reasonably be expected to significantly help determine one or more of the issues raised in the pleadings. (2) The disclosure or production of a record under this Division is not, by reason of that fact alone, to be considered as an agreement or acknowledgment that the record is admissible or relevant and material.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 5.2:1 Rule 5.2 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 5.2. 1. Relevant and Material In Stringam Denecky LLP v. Sun Media Corporation, 2017 ABQB 687, 2017 CarswellAlta 2324, 60 Alta. L.R. (6th) 301, 41 C.C.L.T. (4th) 279, 11 C.P.C. (8th) 123, [2017] A.J. No. 1171, Justice B. Browne said: 12 In Dow Chemical Canada ULC v Nova Chemicals Corp, 2014 ABCA 244 at para 17, 577 AR 335, the Court of Appeal said that, for the purposes of Rule 5.2(1), “relevance is primarily determined by the pleadings, whereas materiality relates to whether the information can help, directly or indirectly, to prove a fact in issue”. 13 Specifically regarding materiality, the Court said: 19 … There is no fixed standard of what is “material”. An element of judgment is required, and questioning is not permitted just because some remote and unlikely line of analysis can be advanced. … 21 It is not sufficient for a litigant to show some theoretical line of argument in order to establish “materiality”. [A] judge is fully entitled to reject lines of pretrial discovery that are unrealistic, speculative, or without any air of reality. … At an interlocutory stage of proceedings, the court should not measure counsels' proposed line of argument too finely: Weatherill, [2003] A.J. No. 88 at para 16. But that does not mean that a proposed line of questioning must be accepted at face value. 14 Earlier, in NAC Constructors Ltd v Alberta Capital Region Wastewater Commission, 2006 ABCA 246, [2006] A.J. No. 1051 (QL) at para 13, the Court of Appeal explained materiality this way: The materiality of evidence refers to its pertinency or weight in relation to the issue it is adduced to prove: Black's Law Dictionary, (6th ed. 1990). Facts or documents may be relevant within Rule 186.1 [now Rule 5.2(1)], but, either alone or in combination with other evidence, be of no significant help to the examining party in proving or disproving a fact in issue. In Terrigno v. Butzner, 2023 ABCA 124, the Court said: [9] Relevance is determined primarily by the pleadings and materiality relates to whether the information can help, directly or indirectly, to prove a fact in issue: Dow Chemical at para 17. There is no fixed standard as to what is material and an element of judgment is required: Dow Chemical at para 19. See also McNabb v. Skinner, 2024 ABCA 355 at paragraphs 18-21. In Forestburg (Village) v. Austin Carroll Pool Construction Ltd., 2024 ABKB 587, Justice Loparco gave this explanation: [23] Relevance is primarily determined by the pleadings as the allegations within the pleadings determine the issues within the action. Whether something is relevant will depend on the issues identified/raised. All pleadings must be considered when assessing relevance: Geophysical Service Incorporated v Edison SPA, 2024 ABKB 27 [Geophysical Service] at para 9; Dow Chemical Canada Inc. v Nova Chemicals Corp., 2014 ABCA 244 [Dow Chemical] at para 17. [24] Materiality is assessed by whether the information in question can significantly help to prove a fact in issue either directly or indirectly. Judgment must be exercised when assessing whether information sought is material: Geophysical Service at para 10; Dow Chemical at para 19. [25] Courts should not be overly strict in assessing relevance and materiality: In deciding whether a particular document is material, one must take a very pragmatic view, viewing the situation from the perspective of the party who must prove the fact in question. At an interlocutory stage of proceedings, the Court should not measure counsels' proposed line of argument too finely; if counsel can disclose a rational strategy in which the disputed document plays a material part, that should be sufficient. Again, it must be remembered that the purpose of the Rule was to avoid abusive, excessive, and unnecessarily expensive discovery, not to cut off legitimate lines of inquiry: McDiarmaid Estate v Alberta, 2022 ABCA 247 at para 29 [McDiarmaid], citing Weatherill Estate v Weatherill, 2003 ABQB 69 at para 16 [Weatherill]. See also Geophysical Service at paras 12 and 14; Dow Chemical at para 21; Goold v Allen, 2023 ABKB 66 at para 16. [26] In Geophysical Service, Justice Horner summarized the burden that the party seeking disclosure must meet: 13. A party that seeks to compel disclosure must therefore show some reason why the fact at issue could reasonably be expected to help determine one or more issues. This burden has been described in several ways: • “ …the [party] need only show a plausible line of argument.”: Kaddoura at para 14. • “…some underlying foundation on which [the party] is basing its allegations…”: Tirecraft Group Inc (Receiver of) v High Park Holdings ULC, 2010 ABQB 653 at para 26. • “Some evidence is required…There must be some underlying factual foundation … ”: Burns at para 28. • “ … if counsel can disclose a rational strategy in which the disputed document plays a material part, that should be sufficient”: Weatherill at para 18. 14. The burden is not intended to be onerous. At the production stage of litigation, the court should not measure the parties' proposed line of argument “too finely”: Dow at para 21 citing Weatherill at para 16. The rules are intended to prevent abusive and/or excessive discovery processes, not to cut off legitimate lines of inquiry: Weatherill at para 16. The party seeking disclosure does not need to prove conclusively that the information will be of any assistance to them: Kaddoura at para 14. In Toronto Dominion Bank v. Suitel Canada Executive Suites Corp., 2012 ABQB 699, 2012 CarswellAlta 2082, 549 A.R. 43, Justice Gates said, at paragraphs 12-13: 12 The wording of Rule 5.2(1) of the new Rules of Court is identical to the wording of the former Rule 186.1. As such, case authority interpreting the former provision is applicable to the proper interpretation of the new provision. 13 Under the old Rule 186.1, oral examination for discovery was confined to eliciting primary facts which are directly at issue or facts from which the existence of primary facts may be inferred directly. In either instance, the question is to be determined by reference to the issues raised by the pleadings. (See NAC Constructors Ltd. v. Alberta Capital Region Wasterwater Commission, 2006 ABCA 246 at para. 11.13.) In Patrick Burns Estate Memorial Trust (Trustee of) v. P. Burns Resources Ltd., 2015 ABQB 459 (Master), Master Robertson gave this summary of the law: 26 In an examination under rule 5.2 to determine whether a question is “relevant and material”, the starting point is to look at the pleadings: Tirecraft Group Inc. (Receiver of) v. High Park Holdings ULC, 2010 ABQB 653 at paragraph 11. 27 It is not just some aspect of the pleadings in isolation, but all of the pleadings that the court must examine when deciding this issue: Hepworth v. Canadian Equestrian Federation, 277 A.R. 138 (C.A. 2000) at para. 7, as cited in Stone Sapphire Ltd. v. Trans-Global Communications Group Inc., 2007 ABQB 238 at paragraph 63. 28 But the inquiry does not end at the pleadings. Some evidence is required. The “Court must be cautious not to allow the applicant to go on a fishing expedition to find some evidence to support the allegations it is making”: Tirecraft at para. 26, quoting Franco v. Hackett, 2000 ABQB 241 (M.C.). There must be some underlying factual foundation on which the allegation is based in the first place: Tirecraft at para. 26. To determine whether the information sought could reasonably be expected to significantly help determine one or more of the issues raised in the pleadings, or to ascertain evidence that could reasonably be expected to significantly help determine one or more of the issues raised in the pleadings, we look at the evidentiary basis. 29 Accordingly, in an enquiry as to whether a particular record must be produced, or a particular question must be answered, the court would normally expect to see some evidence. Normally the evidence in support of an application such as this involves correspondence between counsel that has been sent after counsel has reviewed the opponent's affidavit of records, asking for production of a certain body of records that relates to the dispute; or the transcript leading up to the request for information or the production of a record giving a context to the request; or an affidavit from the applicant explaining the background of the dispute, and why a particular record should be produced or a question answered. See also Case v. Canaccord Genuity Corp., 2019 ABQB 257, 2019 CarswellAlta 694, 91 Alta. L.R. (6th) 274 (Master) at paragraphs 6–9. In Hunka v. Degner, 2011 ABQB 195, 2011 CarswellAlta 472, the Plaintiffs brought an application for an order compelling the disclosure of certain financial records of the Defendants. Justice Gill said, at paragraph 40: “The relevant Rules are Rules 5.1(1) and 5.2(1). …” At paragraphs 41–47, Gill, J. said: 41 The principles outlined by the Court of Appeal in Mustard v. Brache, 2006 ABCA 265 in regard to former Rule 186.1 are still applicable. At paragraphs 10 to 12: [10]… The rule makes clear that the parties' pleadings are the basis for determining relevance and materiality. [11] Discovery of records is now confined to eliciting facts of primary relevance, i.e., facts that are directly in issue, or of secondary relevance, i.e., facts from which the existence of the primary facts may be directly inferred. Both primary and secondary relevance are determined by reference to the issues raised by the pleadings. Records seeking information that could reasonably be expected to lead to facts or records of secondary relevance need not be produced. [12] In addition to being relevant within the meaning of Rule 186.1, records must also be material, that is, they must be reasonably expected to significantly help determine one or more of the issues raised in the pleadings. The materiality of evidence refers to its pertinency or weight in relation to the issue it is adduced to prove: Black's Law Dictionary, (6th ed. 1990). Records may be relevant within Rule 186.1, but, either alone or in combination with other evidence, be of no significant help to the examining party in proving a fact in issue: NAC Constructors Ltd. v. Alberta Capital Region Wastewater Commission, 2006 ABCA 246 (CanLII), 2006 ABCA 246, at para. 13. 42 The approach outlined by Mr. Justice Slatter in Weatherill (Estate of) v. Weatherill, 2003 ABQB 69 at paragraphs 16 and 17 is appropriate to this case: [16]… At an interlocutory stage of proceedings, the Court should not measure counsels' proposed line of argument too finely; if counsel can disclose a rational strategy in which the disputed document plays a material part, that should be sufficient. Again it must be remembered that the purpose of the Rule was to avoid abusive, excessive, and unnecessarily expensive discovery, not to cut off legitimate lines of inquiry. [17] That relevance is determined by the pleadings, while materiality is more a matter of proof can be seen by the wording of the Rule. The Rule talks about records that can “help determine” an issue, or that can “ascertain evidence” that will determine an issue. These are words of proof, and materiality must be determined with that in mind. 43 The pleadings in this action raise numerous causes of action in relation to the Waiward Companies including shareholder oppression, breach of contract, interference with contractual relations, unjust enrichment, and claims for constructive trust. The remedies sought include damages, a buyout of shares, transfer of shares, rectification of the share registry, redemption of shares and repayment of shareholder loans. 44 The documents requested by the Plaintiffs are set out in Appendix “A” of this judgment. They include financial statements of the corporate defendants, major contract documents and documents showing shareholder transactions. Some of the documents requested to be produced include financial documents which the plaintiff's expert considers necessary to conduct a valuation of the shares. 45 The documents in Appendix A appear relevant and material to the claims and allegations raised in the Statement of Claim and as set out in 5.2(1) could reasonably be expected: (a) to significantly help determine one or more of the issues raised in the pleadings, or (b) to ascertain evidence that could reasonably be expected to significantly help determine one or more of the issues raised in the pleadings. These documents should be disclosed. 46 In addition disclosure would be in accordance with the purposes outlined in Rule 5.1(1). 47 The Defendants are not however required to provide regular financial or operational records on a daily or monthly basis. The records to be provided are those which provide a “snapshot” of the companies at a relevant point in time (eg: a year end). In Canadian Natural Resources Ltd. v. ShawCor Ltd., 2013 ABQB 230, 2013 CarswellAlta 496, 559 A.R. 66, 90 Alta. L.R. (5th) 169, Chief Justice Wittmann said, at paragraph 18: 18 The parties agree on the principles governing the disclosure and production of records in an affidavit of records. Relevance and materiality are determined by reference to the issues raised in the pleadings: Liu v. West Edmonton Mall Property Inc. (2000), 279 A.R. 305 (Q.B.) at paras. 19–22. A record is relevant if it elicits facts of primary relevance (those directly in issue) or facts of secondary relevance (facts from which the existence of the primary facts in issue may be directly inferred). A record is material if it is reasonably expected to significantly help determine one or more of the issues raised in the pleadings: Hunka v. Degner, 2011 ABQB 195 at para. 41. Canadian Natural Resources Ltd. v. ShawCor Ltd., 2013 ABQB 230, 2013 CarswellAlta 496, 559 A.R. 66, 90 Alta. L.R. (5th) 169, was overturned on other grounds (see: 2014 ABCA 289), but the above quote was not commented upon adversely. In Dow Chemical Canada Inc. v. Nova Chemicals Corp., 2015 ABQB 2, 2015 CarswellAlta 9, Chief Justice Wittmann said, at paragraph 15: [15] The Court of Appeal in Dow Chemical Canada ULC v Nova Chemicals Corporation, 2014 ABCA 244 (CanLII) at paragraph 17, after quoting ARC 5.2(1), indicated that relevance is primarily determined with reference to the pleadings, but materiality concerns whether the information can assist directly or indirectly to prove a fact in issue (para. 17). The point is that the scope of document production or production of records as it is now called, and questioning, formerly oral examination for discovery, has been narrowed since 1999. Secondly, it is to be remembered that it is the legal obligation of the party producing records or delivering an Affidavit of Records to decide what is relevant and material and what is not. That is not to say that differences cannot arise. But it is the obligation of a party, assisted by counsel, where available, to disclose relevant and material records. In Canadian Natural Resources Ltd. v. Arcelormittal Tubular Products Roman S.A., 2013 ABQB 439, 2013 CarswellAlta 1501, 558 A.R. 361, 88 Alta. L.R. (5th) 149, Madam Justice Hughes, having noted that “[u]nder the 2010 reworking of the Rules of Court, Rule 186.1 was replaced by Rule 5.2, which is identical to Rule 186.1” (paragraph 22), said, at paragraphs 24-25: 24 The Court of Appeal summarized the law relating to Rule 186.1 in both Mustard v. Brache, 2006 ABCA 265, 397 AR 361 [“Mustard”], and NAC Constructors Ltd. v. Alberta Capital Region Wastewater Commission, 2006 ABCA 246, 412 AR 272 [“NAC”]. Mustard spoke to the applicability of the Rule to document discovery; NAC set out the same principles respecting questioning at paras 11–13: In Johnston v. Bryant et al. (2003), 327 A.R. 378, 296 W.A.C. 378, 2003 ABCA 169, the Court observed at para. 12 that “Rule 186.1 is intended to limit the scope of discovery from what it was under previous rules”. It is “designed to limit … tertiary lines of inquiry”: Auer v. Lionstone Holdings Inc. et al. (2005), 363 A.R. 84, 243 W.A.C. 84, 2005 ABCA 78, at para. 30, citing Hiltz v. Public Trustee (Alta) (2002), 303 A.R. 25, 273 W.A.C. 25, 2002 ABCA 29. In Hepworth v. Canadian Equestrian Federation et al. (2000), 277 A.R. 138, 248 W.A.C. 138, 2000 ABCA 327, at para. 12, the Court held the disputed questions were proper under both the new and old discovery Rules. Issues raised in the pleadings are the basis for determining both relevance and materiality: D'Elia v. Dansereau (2000), 267 A.R. 157, 2000 ABQB 425, at para. 17. Oral examination for discovery is now confined to eliciting facts of primary relevance, that is, facts that are directly in issue, or of secondary relevance, that is, facts from which the existence of the primary facts may be directly inferred. Both primary and secondary relevance are determined by reference to the issues raised by the pleadings. Questions seeking information that could reasonably be expected to lead to facts or records of secondary relevance (that is, questions asking for information that is only of tertiary relevance) need no longer be answered. In addition to being relevant within the meaning of Rule 186.1, information sought on discovery must be material, that is, be reasonably expected to “significantly” help determine one or more of the issues raised in the pleadings. The materiality of evidence refers to its pertinency or weight in relation to the issue it is adduced to prove: Black's Law Dictionary, (6th Ed. 1990). Facts or documents may be relevant within Rule 186.1, but, either alone or in combination with other evidence, be of no significant help to the examining party in proving or disproving a fact in issue. As Slatter J. observed in Weatherill Estate v. Weatherill et al., (2003) 337 A.R. 180, 2003 ABQB 69, at para. 17, “… relevance is determined by the pleadings while materiality is more a matter of proof …”. See also Tolko Industries Ltd. v. Railink Ltd. et al. (2003), 333 A.R. 270, 14 Alta. L.R. (4th) 388, 2003 ABQB 349, at para. 6 [original emphasis]. 25 Judicial interpretation of Rule 186.1 remains applicable to new Rule 5.2: Hunka v. Degner, 2011 ABQB 195 at para 41, and Toronto-Dominion Bank v. Suitel Canada Executive Suites Corp, 2012 ABQB 699 at para 12. In M. (A.) v. Matthews, 2011 ABQB 187, 2011 CarswellAlta 477, Veit, J. said, at paragraph 12: 12 Rule 5.2(1) states that a record is relevant and material only if the record could reasonably be expected to significantly help determine one or more of the issues raised in the pleadings, or to ascertain evidence that could reasonably be expected to significantly help determine one or more of the issues raised in the pleadings. This rule is much narrower than its predecessor. Not only is tertiary relevance excluded, but, more importantly here, the materiality or weight of the evidence must be addressed with a view to determining whether the record will significantly help to determine one of the issues raised in the pleadings. Verville, J. in Araam Inc. v. Aman Building Corp., 2011 ABQB 631, 2011 CarswellAlta 1757, [2011] A.J. No. 1097 referred with approval to the above quote from M. (A.) v. Matthews, 2011 ABQB 187, 2011 CarswellAlta 477. However, Madam Justice Hughes, in Canadian Natural Resources Ltd. v. Arcelormittal Tubular Products Roman S.A., 2013 ABQB 439, 2013 CarswellAlta 1501, 558 A.R. 361, 88 Alta. L.R. (5th) 149, said that “predecessor” rule referred to in M. (A.) v. Matthews, 2011 ABQB 187, 2011 CarswellAlta 477, was the old Rule which preceded Rule 186.1. At paragraph 23 of Canadian Natural Resources Ltd. v. Arcelormittal Tubular Products Roman S.A., Justice Hughes said: 23 The Defendant Vass, in its Brief of Argument, cites Mahamed v. Matthews, 2011 ABQB 187 at para 12 [“Mahamed”], as authority for the proposition that Rule 5.2 is “much narrower than its predecessor.” I find the “predecessor” referred to in Mahamed was not Rule 186.1, but rather Rule 186.1's predecessor, which allowed for discovery of all evidence “touching on the matters in question.” There is no doubt that the 1999 change to the current wording was, as noted by the Court of Appeal in Johnston v. Bryant, 2003 ABCA 169, 327 AR 378 at para 12, “intended to limit the scope of discovery from what it was under previous rules.” In Geophysical Service Inc. v. NWest Energy Corp., 2017 ABQB 232, 2017 CarswellAlta 565, Justice D. B. Nixon provided this summary of the law relating to disclosure of information: 18 Disclosure of information is governed by Part 5 of the Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010. … 2. — The Starting Point—The Pleadings 19 In litigation, the starting point in respect of any decision to compel the production of information is the pleadings: Araam Inc v Aman Building Corporation, 2011 ABQB 631 at para 14; Mustard v Brache, 2006 ABCA 265 at para 10; and Weatherill (Estate) v Weatherill, 2003 ABQB 69 at paras 16 and 17. 20 Questioning under the Rules may only seek facts of primary or secondary relevance. Facts of primary relevance are those directly in issue. Arcelormittal Tubular Products Roman S.A., 2013 ABQB 439, 2013 CarswellAlta 1501, 558 A.R. 361, 88 Alta. L.R. (5th) 149, Hughes, J. said, at paragraph26: 26 The Defendants have argued that the materials sought by CNRL are “tertiary” evidence. As noted by Slatter J. in Weatherill Estate v. paragraphs.text: (1) The Court may modify or waive any right or power under a rule in this Part or make any order warranted in the circumstances if (a) a person acts or threatens to act in a manner that is vexatious, evasive, abusive, oppressive, improper or tediously lengthy, or (b) the expense, delay, danger or difficulty in complying with a rule would be grossly disproportionate to the likely benefit. (2) In addition to making a procedural order, the Court may do any one or more of the following: (a) make a costs award under Part 10 or require an advance payment against costs payable, or both; (b) increase or decrease the amount of interest to which a person is entitled; (c) order future questioning to be conducted before a judge, applications judge or person designated by the Court; (d) make any other order respecting the action or an application or proceeding the Court considers necessary in the circumstances. Alta. Reg. 136/2022, s. 1(2)

Burns Resources Ltd. V. Honourable Patrick Burns Memorial Trust (Trustee of), 2015 ABCA 390, the Court of Appeal considered the question of “whether a party is entitled to the usual procedures for production of documents and questioning prior to the hearing of an application for summary dismissal.” The Court said: 7 We agree with the chambers judge that the Alberta Rules of Court do not require as a default position that the usual procedures relating to document production and questioning under Part 5 be put on hold pending an application for summary judgment or summary dismissal. Rule 5. 3 provides that the Court may modify or waive any right or power under that Part if “the expense, delay, danger or difficulty in complying with a rule would be grossly proportionate to the likely benefit”. That provision leaves the matter in the discretion of the court; it does not mandate that the operation of Part 5 be suspended in the face of an application for summary judgment. … [8]… Where the nature of the action is such that much of the evidence supporting the cause of action is likely to be in the sole possession of the defendants, the plaintiff is more likely to require access to disclosure of documents and questioning to be able to make full answer to any subsequent application for summary judgment. 9 Whether document production and questioning should proceed prior to the hearing of a summary judgment application is a discretionary decision under the rules. That discretion must be exercised giving due consideration to the purposes of Part 5, which include facilitating resolution of issues and discouraging “conduct that unnecessarily or improperly delays proceedings or unnecessarily increases their costs”: Rule 5.1(1). There will undoubtedly be cases in which the circumstances of the proceedings dictate that a summary judgment application should proceed without the additional time and expense required to satisfy all of the disclosure requirements of Part 5. 2. Written Interrogatories In Dunn v. Dunn (2001), 297 A.R. 365 (Q.B.) examinations for discovery had become somewhat acrimonious between counsel. The Plaintiff sought an order permitting her to conduct further examinations by way of interrogatories. In dismissing the application, Lee J. said, at pp. 370-372: As a result of rule 216.1, if the plaintiff wishes to proceed by way of written interrogatories, the plaintiff bears the onus of establishing either that the defendant has acted or threatened to act in a manner that is vexatious, evasive, abusive, oppressive, improper or prolix; or that the expense, delay, danger or difficulty in proceeding by way of oral discovery would be grossly disproportionate to the likely benefit. In the current case, counsel for the defendant Mr. Dunn, has at various times shown great frustration and has clearly been irritated by the somewhat slow discovery process and by opposing counsel's objections. Some of defence counsel's comments have been inappropriate and unfortunate, there is, however, no evidence that the defendant has acted or threatened to act in a manner that is vexatious, evasive, abusive, oppressive, improper or prolix. The defendant has been willing and eager to proceed with examinations under the Rules of Court. As a consequence, the plaintiff is limited to attempting to establish that the expense, delay, danger or difficulty in proceeding by way of oral discovery would be grossly disproportionate to the likely benefit. Further, even if the plaintiff can meet the requirements under rule 216.1(1)(b), the plaintiff must still establish that the most appropriate means to deal with the perceived inadequacies in the traditional discovery procedures would be to order written interrogatories under rules 216.1(2)(j). Application of Rule 216.1 a) Interrogatories The parties acknowledge that the present method and pace of examination is not ideal. Interrogatories would very likely quicken the pace of these seemingly interminable discoveries and reduce the costs these parties have been incurring as a result of the friction between them. However, interrogatories are appropriate mainly where “… the information or admissions sought are clerical, lengthy or technical, and where the information exists in various disconnected places in the answering parties records”. G.D. Cudmore, Choate on Discoveries (2nd Ed.) (Toronto: Carswell, current) at 4 - 3, citing Plumrose Inc. v. A & A Foods Ltd. (1994), 32 C.P.C. (3d) 230 (B.C. S.C. [In Chambers]). Conversely, because written interrogatories do not provide an opportunity to counsel to observe the opposite party, to assess his or her ability as a witness, or to ferret out weakness, they are not appropriate where the questions to be put to the witness are of a general nature and where the questions will take a more narrative form: This analysis is particularly applicable to the choice between examinations for discovery and interrogatories. Generally speaking, issues involving extensive research, such as precise chronologies or exhaustive lists, would seem to be more appropriate for the more expansive time-frame permitted by interrogatories than for a more confrontational, time-pressured examination for discovery. Conversely, questions requiring a narrative answer are much more likely to remain in focus at an examination for discovery, where counsel can expand on and limit the witness's answers as appropriate. Roitman v. Chan, [1994] B.C.J. No. 2462 at p. 4 (Master). Further, there are additional difficulties that accompany an examination by way of written interrogatories, such as: • The answers will inevitably be drafted by opposing counsel, and not be the words of the party. Answers will be ambiguous; • Written interrogatories provide an opportunity for opposing counsel to find many objections to the questions, or their form, possibly resulting in time consuming motions; and • The procedure is cumbersome and time consuming. In this case, the questions that will be put to the plaintiff at her examination will be of a general narrative nature and will not be clerical, lengthy or technical. To attempt to conduct such an examination by way of interrogatories would be time consuming and expensive. Further, to conduct examinations by way of interrogatories would deprive the defendant of his ability to observe the witness and to pursue lines of questioning that will inevitably develop throughout the course of an oral examination. As a result of the concerns noted above, to proceed by way of written interrogatories at this time would be inappropriate, expensive, time consuming and would unnecessarily prejudice the defendant's right to fully examine the plaintiff. As a consequence, the most appropriate way to proceed in this case is by way of oral discoveries. If counsel for the defendant, however, continues to demonstrate inappropriate impatience and frustration thereby causing unnecessary anxiety in the plaintiff, Ms. Dunn, the court can and will deal with the matter again this time either by revisiting the use of written interrogatories; or under rule 216.1(2)(n) by way of an order providing for supervision of the continued examination of Ms. Dunn by a judge, master, commissioner, clerk or referee. Such an order or such written interrogatories would strike the appropriate balance between the defendant's right to examine the plaintiff in person, and the difficulties associated with the plaintiff's hearing and health impediments. This is also not to suggest that plaintiff's counsel has conducted himself properly at all times either, as further evidenced by the fact that both of his motions are now being dismissed. In Cardinal v. 361881 Alberta Inc., 2001 ABQB 51, 2001 CarswellAlta 146, 298 A.R. 15, it would appear that Sanderman J. used Rule 216.1(2)(j) though he did not specifically refer to it. A motor vehicle accident claimed the life of a young man. His parents commenced an action, but the father found the whole matter too distressing so he withdrew from the action, leaving the mother as the plaintiff. The defendants sought an order under Rule 201 to examine for discovery the father as a person for whose benefit the case was being prosecuted. Sanderman J. granted the order, but only permitted the examination to occur by interrogatories. At p. 17, His Lordship said: Mr. Cardinal has been greatly effected (sic) by the death of his son. He has withdrawn from this lawsuit because it is too painful for him to continue with it. He is extremely reluctant to have anything to do with it because of the terrible memories it continues to reinforce. The type of questions that the applicant wants to put to Mr. Cardinal do not require his personal attendance. A balancing of the applicant's need to get information and Mr. Cardinal's need for solitude in relation to this matter permits me to direct that he need not personally appear for examination. It would be insensitive and cruel to have this grieving individual journey to Edmonton from his rural residence in northeastern Alberta in order to answer questions about a continuing painful experience when the same result can be achieved through the use of written interrogatories. I will not direct Mr. Cardinal to appear. I direct that counsel for the applicant provide questions in a written form to counsel for the plaintiffs, and that answers be provided within 45 days of receiving the questions in a written form. It would appear that Sanderman J. concluded that Rule 216.1(1)(b) was satisfied in that the “difficulty” for the father occasioned by him attending examinations for discovery would be disproportionate to the benefit thereby obtained by the defendant. In Grebely v. Economincal Mutual Ins., 2003 ABQB 547, 2003 CarswellAlta 889, the plaintiff Grebely suffered from possible cardiac problems. There was medical evidence that the stress of oral examinations for discovery might “place him at increased risk of cardiac consequences”. Grebely sought an order that his examination for discovery begin with written interrogatories after which there would be oral examinations for discovery for one or two days. In granting the order under Rule 216.1(1), Madam Justice Kent said (at paragraphs 5-6): [5] In my view, the word ‘danger’ in Rule 216.1(1) is intended to address the kind of situation before me. I have a discretion to relieve against the requirement of oral discoveries in appropriate circumstances. Although I must be careful not to visit upon the Defendants Mr. Grebely's personal health problems, it seems to me that a combination of written interrogatories and oral discovery achieves all the purposes for which witness discovery is intended. The written interrogatories will allow the Defendants to obtain information about the Plaintiffs' claim. The oral discovery which the Defendants have already had and will have will allow the Defendants to assess Mr. Grebely as a witness and to obtain admissions. I acknowledge that as a Plaintiff it is Mr. Grebely's action to prosecute or not. It should be the rare case when Rule 216.1 is invoked because of the health condition of a plaintiff where that condition is not related to the issues in the action. This is one of these rare cases, given the serious nature of Mr. Grebely's condition and the fact the written interrogatories do not prejudice the Defendants' ability to defend. [6] Two issues remain. The first is how to divide up what is appropriate for interrogatories and what should be left to oral discovery. Generally speaking, the written interrogatories should address all questions which can legitimately be classified as information-seeking. A good example in most actions is the particularization of the damage claim. Counsel should attempt as much as possible to use written interrogatories to minimize the time needed for oral discoveries. I am not going to limit the oral discoveries by time. Should any disputes arise, they can be addressed at case management meetings. 3. “Counsel's Eyes Only” Orders In Murphy Oil Co. v. Predator Corp., 2002 ABQB 992, 2002 CarswellAlta 1605, 328 A.R. 308, an application was brought by the plaintiffs for an order restricting the other parties' Rule 188 access rights to documents produced by the plaintiffs under their Rule 187 obligations. As described by McMahon J., the order sought “has been referred to as a ‘counsel's eyes only’ order. Its impact would preclude the individual and corporate defendants from seeing the documents or being told of their contents or being able to attend at examinations for discovery where the documents are discussed.” In dismissing the application, his Lordship said, at pp. 310-313: Rule 188 of the Rules of Court gives a party an unencumbered right to inspection of the opposite party's records. Both parties here recognize, however, this Court's inherent jurisdiction to impose restrictive conditions on inspections to prevent abuse. To a degree, that jurisdiction was codified in 1995 by Rule 216.1. … Both parties recite the implied undertaking that: A party who seeks discovery of documents gets it on condition that he will make use of them only for the purpose of that action, and for no other purpose. Riddick's Case, [1977] 3 All E.R. 677 at 688. The applicable principles were summarized by Brandon, L.J., in Church of Scientology of California v. Department of Health and Social Security and Others, [1979] 3 All E.R. 97 (C.A.), at 113: 1. A party to litigation has a prima facie right of unrestricted inspection of the documents of which discovery has been made by the other party so far as may be necessary to dispose fairly of the case or for saving costs. 2. A party is not entitled to use his right of inspection for any collateral purpose. 3. If it is shown that there is a real risk of a party using his right for a collateral purpose, the court has power to impose restrictions on such right in order to prevent or discourage him from doing so. The burden of justifying the need for an order precluding inspection of records by the parties themselves lies in the party seeking the order. Such an order is rarely given and the applicant's burden is heavy. … The order sought here would preclude the defendants or their employees from seeing the records, being told of their contents, discussing them with counsel or experts or attending at examination for discovery or trial when those records are discussed. They could not review parts of the trial transcripts for the purposes of deciding upon an appeal. Indeed, if the records are significant—a fact which will not finally be known until judgment is in—they may not be able to read parts of the reasons for judgment discussing that evidence. The fundamental principle of open justice and the right of a litigant to hear and meet the case opposite is compromised when these orders are given. Unusual circumstances may compel such order where the risk of abuse is virtually apparent such as in Church of Scientology of California, supra. Similarly, in patent and trade secret cases where litigation fairness will not be lost by precluding a party from access to relevant evidence, such orders may be available. Here, the relevance of the records is acknowledged by Murphy. The amended defence puts Murphy's evaluation and its evaluation technique squarely in issue. The statement of claim alleges that the defendants used wrongly obtained pressure data to formulate its bids. One of the defences is that the pressure data was not even used by Murphy in its evaluations. Another is that Murphy failed to properly evaluate the lands and so did not bid enough or, in one case, bid too much. In both cases to make out their defence, the defendants will need to know Murphy's evaluation techniques. If, as Murphy's deponent says, the information could be used to assess how Murphy may bid in the future (and how it did bid at the land sales in question) then its probative value to the defence is obvious. Another of the considerations before me is the lack of timeliness of this application. The parties are competitors in the oil and gas exploration business. Both parties analysed data available to them and prepared bids for lands, which bids led to this litigation. Yet Murphy did not bring this application until after the defendants had produced their records, including geological maps and cross-sections; and until Murphy, as plaintiff, had conducted some 18 days of examinations for discovery of the corporate defendant's officer. Much of that discovery is said to have related to the defendants' interpretation of its own data. The interests of litigation fairness must be weighed against business confidentiality concerns. When both sides have confidential records and one has complied with the general rule of inspection, it would be unfair to only then permit the other party to advance a confidentiality claim to its records. … In the result the fairness and integrity of the trial system would be compromised by the order sought in these circumstances. The implied undertaking is sufficient. The parties should be reminded that a breach of that undertaking may be found to be a contempt of court and can lead to injunctive relief and damages. In Phoenix Technology Services v. Braisher, 2007 ABQB 261, 2007 CarswellAlta 514, 74 Alta. L.R. (4th) 328, Madam Justice Martin considered Rule 216.1 and “counsel/expert eyes only” orders. She specifically commented on Justice McMahon's decision in Murphy Oil Co. v. Predator Corp., 2002 ABQB 992, 2002 CarswellAlta 1605, 328 A.R. 308. At pp. 334–336, her Ladyship said: 18 Confidentiality orders of the nature sought here have been made in Alberta. They are frequently made by consent, but Wachowich J. (as he then was), granted a contested Counsel/Expert's Eyes Only Order in Ed Miller Sales and Rentals v. Caterpillar Tractor Co. (1986), 43 Alta.L.R. (2d) 299 (Q.B.). He expressly adopted the principles set out in Church of Scientology of California v. Department of Health and Social Security, [1979] 1 W.L.R. 732 (C.A.), wherein Brandon L.J. held, at p. 743: …[T]he principles applicable are, in my view, as follows: 1. A party to litigation has a prima facie right of unrestricted inspection of the documents of which discovery has been made by the other party so far as may be necessary to dispose fairly of the case or for saving costs. 2. A party is not entitled to use his right of inspection for any collateral purpose. 3. If it is shown that there is a real risk of a party using his right for a collateral purpose, the Court has power to impose restrictions on such right in order to prevent or discourage him from doing so. I think that this power is derived from the inherent jurisdiction of the court to prevent abuse of its process… 19 The prima face right to the unrestricted inspection of documents of which discovery has been made, and the implied undertaking not to use this right for any collateral purpose are well established. Wachowich J. recognized that exceptions to the general rule of unrestricted inspection should be rare, at p.301: In the majority of cases, the implied undertaking is sufficient. The next level of cases is where the Court may require a formal undertaking by the party or their Counsel not to misuse the information. Finally, the extreme position is composed of a “small hard core of cases” where additional precautions are necessary to ensure no abuse of the discovery process… 20 In Wirth Ltd. v. Acadia Pipe & Supply Corp. (1991), 113 A.R. 298 (Q.B.), in considering whether there was an implied undertaking not to use information obtained through the discovery process for any purpose outside of the litigation, Lutz J. noted that a non-disclosure order may be sought where there are special circumstances. Citing Ed Miller Sales and Church of Scientology, he suggested that the test for a non- disclosure order is that of a “real risk”. 21 Ed Miller Sales and Wirth were decided prior to the introduction of Rule 216.1 to the Alberta Rules of Court in 1996. The relevant portions of the rule provide: 216.1 (1) The Court may modify or waive any right or power under this Part, on terms or otherwise, or may impose terms on any party, where … (b) the expense, delay, danger or difficulty in complying fully would be grossly disproportionate to the likely benefit. (2) Terms imposed under subrule (1) may, without limiting the generality of subrule (1), be made in respect of the following: … (e) production of or access to documents, whether or not they are referred to in any pleading, particular or affidavit; (o) a confidentiality order. 22 Phoenix points out that while parties may have consented to similar orders in the past, this would be the first time a confidentiality order is approved judicially under Rule 216.1. The introduction of Rule 216.1 in 1996 raises the question of whether it changed the test from “real risk”, as set out in Ed Miller Sales, to “grossly disproportionate danger,” which is the language used in the Rule. The foregoing review of the jurisprudence demonstrates that the term “grossly disproportionate” was not part of the common-law test for confidentiality orders. In certain cases, courts have spoken of “balancing,” or a “real risk.” 23 McMahon J. considered an application for a confidentiality order under Rule 216.1 in Murphy Oil Co. v. Predator Corp., [2002] A.J. No. 1531 (Q.B.), 2002 ABQB 992. He noted, at para. 5, that Rule 216.1 codified, to a degree, the Court's inherent jurisdiction to impose restrictive conditions upon the inspection of the opposite party's records. He went on to find, at para.16, that in the circumstances before him, the evidence did not establish “unusual circumstances or real risk of abuse.” While this suggests that McMahon J. was applying a different test from the “grossly disproportionate danger” test set out in the rule, his decision must be viewed in the context of his determination that the applicant had failed to bring evidence that would satisfy the arguably lower threshold of “real risk”, and, importantly, that the application had not been brought in a timely manner because the respondent had already produced information that it considered confidential. In short, Murphy Oil was essentially decided on different grounds and it was not necessary to determine whether Rule 216.1 was a full codification of the Court's jurisdiction in respect of confidentiality orders. 24 There is little to be gained in questioning whether the term “grossly disproportionate” was selected because it was intended to capture existing law or, in the alternative, as an augmentation to existing standards. Those standards were stated in variable terms in any event. What is clear is that the legislature intended that the balance between interests be done under the rubric it selected, being “grossly disproportionate danger.” It is not open to me to rely upon the inherent jurisdiction of this Court to ignore the test set out in the Rule. It is worth noting that in other contexts, the courts in this province have used this standard: Klapstein v. Alberta Mortgage & Housing Corp., [1998] A.J. No. 611 (C.A.), Gouin v. Gouin, [2006] A.J. No. 127 (Q.B.). The pre-1996 jurisprudence remains relevant because it sets out factors to be considered and the competing values at issue. However, the balancing of those interests must be done under the statutory requirement set out in Rule 216.1. Application of the Rule 216.1 Test in the Context of a Confidentiality Order 25 One principle that remains unchanged from the jurisprudence prior to 1996 is that each application for a confidentiality order must be assessed on the basis of the particular circumstances, facts and evidence at hand. The issue in every case will be whether the risk associated with disclosing the information in question is grossly disproportionate to the well recognized merits associated with full disclosure of all relevant information to the parties. A Counsel/Expert Eyes Only Order will be the exception, and the burden is on the applicant to prove, on a balance of probabilities, all requirements of Rule 216.1. 26 The starting point is the fundamental nature of a party's right (whether plaintiff or defendant) to fully know the case against it and to instruct counsel. At the same time, while it is true that these are important considerations, they are considerations which exist in every case. In certain circumstances, the simple assertion of this principle may be all that is necessary to defeat the applicant's claim that disclosure of confidential or proprietary information may expose the applicant to risk grossly disproportionate to the benefit to be obtained from the disclosure. However, when the applicant's evidence is compelling and uncontradicted, and the Court has a discretion to craft a flexible order, the evidentiary burden may shift to the respondent to demonstrate specific prejudice. To put it another way, while the legal burden remains on the applicant to prove a grossly disproportionate danger under Rule 216.1, where the applicant has brought evidence of grossly disproportionate danger and proposes a sufficiently flexible order, it may be incumbent upon a respondent to do more than simply assert that the general principle is full disclosure. Martin J. then noted that it was appropriate to consider the knowledge of the party to whom the disclosure was to be made, the nature of the information to be disclosed. At pp. 336-337, she said: In Warner-Lambert Co. v. Glaxo Laboratories Ltd., [1975] R.P.C 354, a decision of the English Court of Appeal, Buckley L.J. recognized, at pps. 360-361, that the nature of the information, and the knowledge of the parties to whom it might be disclosed in the ordinary course, are relevant considerations: Where a matter in question in an action, being that matter upon which inspection or disclosure will throw light, is of a technical nature, the party seeking discovery may well require inspection by, or disclosure to, technical and professional advisors. If the matter be of a kind on which the party will be likely to be able with the aid of those advisers to form some kind of view of his own, it seems to me that he should normally be allowed to know as much about the facts as his advisers. If, however, the case were one of so esoterically technical a character that even with the help of his expert advisers the party himself could really form no view of his own upon the matter in question but would be bound to act merely upon advice on the technical aspects, disclosure to him of the facts underlying the advice might serve little or no useful purpose. In such a case a court might well be justified in directing disclosure of allegedly secret material only to expert or professional agents of the party seeking discovery on terms that they should not, without further order, pass on any information so obtained to the party himself or anyone else, but should merely advise him in the light of the information so obtained. 28 In the result, Buckley L.J. concluded that it would be appropriate to allow disclosure of proprietary information to the plaintiff. His conclusion was based on evidence before him that the plaintiff's advisors were unable to give meaningful guidance to the plaintiff without disclosing the information, and he limited the disclosure to the “principal executive officer” of the plaintiff corporation alone. 29 The nature of the proposed order is a relevant consideration in weighing the risk of disclosure of confidential information against the benefit of full disclosure. A carefully crafted order that preserves flexibility will reduce the negative impact of the order on the benefits associated with full disclosure to the parties.

361881 Alberta Inc., 2001 ABQB 51, 2001 CarswellAlta 146, 298 A.R.
15, it would appear that Sanderman J. used Rule 216.1(2)(j) though he did not specifically refer to it.
A motor vehicle accident claimed the life of a young man.
His parents commenced an action, but the father found the whole matter too distressing so he withdrew from the action, leaving the mother as the plaintiff.
The defendants sought an order under Rule 201 to examine for discovery the father as a person for whose benefit the case was being prosecuted.
Sanderman J. granted the order, but only permitted the examination to occur by interrogatories.
At p.
17, His Lordship said: Mr.
Cardinal has been greatly effected (sic) by the death of his son.
He has withdrawn from this lawsuit because it is too painful for him to continue with it.
He is extremely reluctant to have anything to do with it because of the terrible memories it continues to reinforce.
The type of questions that the applicant wants to put to Mr.
Cardinal do not require his personal attendance.
A balancing of the applicant's need to get information and Mr.
Cardinal's need for solitude in relation to this matter permits me to direct that he need not personally appear for examination.

It would be insensitive and cruel to have this grieving individual journey to Edmonton from his rural residence in northeastern Alberta in order to answer questions about a continuing painful experience when the same result can be achieved through the use of written interrogatories.
I will not direct Mr.
Cardinal to appear.
I direct that counsel for the applicant provide questions in a written form to counsel for the plaintiffs, and that answers be provided within 45 days of receiving the questions in a written form.

It would appear that Sanderman J. concluded that Rule 216.1(1)(b) was satisfied in that the “difficulty” for the father occasioned by him attending examinations for discovery would be disproportionate to the benefit thereby obtained by the defendant.
In Grebely v.
Economincal Mutual Ins., 2003 ABQB 547, 2003 CarswellAlta 889, the plaintiff Grebely suffered from possible cardiac problems.
There was medical evidence that the stress of oral examinations for discovery might “place him at increased risk of cardiac consequences”.
Grebely sought an order that his examination for discovery begin with written interrogatories after which there would be oral examinations for discovery for one or two days.
In granting the order under Rule 216.1(1), Madam Justice Kent said (at paragraphs 5-6): [5] In my view, the word ‘danger’ in Rule 216.1(1) is intended to address the kind of situation before me.
I have a discretion to relieve against the requirement of oral discoveries in appropriate circumstances.
Although I must be careful not to visit upon the Defendants Mr.
Grebely's personal health problems, it seems to me that a combination of written interrogatories and oral discovery achieves all the purposes for which witness discovery is intended.
The written interrogatories will allow the Defendants to obtain information about the Plaintiffs' claim.
The oral discovery which the Defendants have already had and will have will allow the Defendants to assess Mr.
Grebely as a witness and to obtain admissions.
I acknowledge that as a Plaintiff it is Mr.
Grebely's action to prosecute or not.
It should be the rare case when Rule 216.1 is invoked because of the health condition of a plaintiff where that condition is not related to the issues in the action.
This is one of these rare cases, given the serious nature of Mr.
Grebely's condition and the fact the written interrogatories do not prejudice the Defendants' ability to defend.
[6] Two issues remain.
The first is how to divide up what is appropriate for interrogatories and what should be left to oral discovery.
Generally speaking, the written interrogatories should address all questions which can legitimately be classified as information-seeking.
A good example in most actions is the particularization of the damage claim.
Counsel should attempt as much as possible to use written interrogatories to minimize the time needed for oral discoveries.
I am not going to limit the oral discoveries by time.
Should any disputes arise, they can be addressed at case management meetings.
3. “Counsel's Eyes Only” Orders In Murphy Oil Co. v.
Predator Corp., 2002 ABQB 992, 2002 CarswellAlta 1605, 328 A.R.
308, an application was brought by the plaintiffs for an order restricting the other parties' Rule 188 access rights to documents produced by the plaintiffs under their Rule 187 obligations.
As described by McMahon J., the order sought “has been referred to as a ‘counsel's eyes only’ order.

Its impact would preclude the individual and corporate defendants from seeing the documents or being told of their contents or being able to attend at examinations for discovery where the documents are discussed.” In dismissing the application, his Lordship said, at pp.
310-313: Rule 188 of the Rules of Court gives a party an unencumbered right to inspection of the opposite party's records.
Both parties here recognize, however, this Court's inherent jurisdiction to impose restrictive conditions on inspections to prevent abuse.

To a degree, that jurisdiction was codified in 1995 by Rule 216.1. … Both parties recite the implied undertaking that: A party who seeks discovery of documents gets it on condition that he will make use of them only for the purpose of that action, and for no other purpose.
Riddick's Case, [1977] 3 All E.R.
The applicable principles were summarized by Brandon, L.J., in Church of Scientology of California v.
Department of Health and Social Security and Others, [1979] 3 All E.R.

A party to litigation has a prima facie right of unrestricted inspection of the documents of which discovery has been made by the other party so far as may be necessary to dispose fairly of the case or for saving costs.
A party is not entitled to use his right of inspection for any collateral purpose.

If it is shown that there is a real risk of a party using his right for a collateral purpose, the court has power to impose restrictions on such right in order to prevent or discourage him from doing so.
The burden of justifying the need for an order precluding inspection of records by the parties themselves lies in the party seeking the order.

Such an order is rarely given and the applicant's burden is heavy. … The order sought here would preclude the defendants or their employees from seeing the records, being told of their contents, discussing them with counsel or experts or attending at examination for discovery or trial when those records are discussed.
They could not review parts of the trial transcripts for the purposes of deciding upon an appeal.
Indeed, if the records are significant—a fact which will not finally be known until judgment is in—they may not be able to read parts of the reasons for judgment discussing that evidence.
The fundamental principle of open justice and the right of a litigant to hear and meet the case opposite is compromised when these orders are given.
Unusual circumstances may compel such order where the risk of abuse is virtually apparent such as in Church of Scientology of California, supra.
Similarly, in patent and trade secret cases where litigation fairness will not be lost by precluding a party from access to relevant evidence, such orders may be available.
Here, the relevance of the records is acknowledged by Murphy.
The amended defence puts Murphy's evaluation and its evaluation technique squarely in issue.
The statement of claim alleges that the defendants used wrongly obtained pressure data to formulate its bids.
One of the defences is that the pressure data was not even used by Murphy in its evaluations.
Another is that Murphy failed to properly evaluate the lands and so did not bid enough or, in one case, bid too much.
In both cases to make out their defence, the defendants will need to know Murphy's evaluation techniques.

If, as Murphy's deponent says, the information could be used to assess how Murphy may bid in the future (and how it did bid at the land sales in question) then its probative value to the defence is obvious.
Another of the considerations before me is the lack of timeliness of this application.
The parties are competitors in the oil and gas exploration business.
Both parties analysed data available to them and prepared bids for lands, which bids led to this litigation.

Yet Murphy did not bring this application until after the defendants had produced their records, including geological maps and cross-sections; and until Murphy, as plaintiff, had conducted some 18 days of examinations for discovery of the corporate defendant's officer.
Much of that discovery is said to have related to the defendants' interpretation of its own data.
The interests of litigation fairness must be weighed against business confidentiality concerns.

When both sides have confidential records and one has complied with the general rule of inspection, it would be unfair to only then permit the other party to advance a confidentiality claim to its records. … In the result the fairness and integrity of the trial system would be compromised by the order sought in these circumstances.
The implied undertaking is sufficient.
The parties should be reminded that a breach of that undertaking may be found to be a contempt of court and can lead to injunctive relief and damages.
In Phoenix Technology Services v.
Braisher, 2007 ABQB 261, 2007 CarswellAlta 514, 74 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 328, Madam Justice Martin considered Rule 216.1 and “counsel/expert eyes only” orders.
She specifically commented on Justice McMahon's decision in Murphy Oil Co. v.
Predator Corp., 2002 ABQB 992, 2002 CarswellAlta 1605, 328 A.R.
At pp.
334–336, her Ladyship said: 18 Confidentiality orders of the nature sought here have been made in Alberta.
They are frequently made by consent, but Wachowich J.
(as he then was), granted a contested Counsel/Expert's Eyes Only Order in Ed Miller Sales and Rentals v.
Caterpillar Tractor Co.
He expressly adopted the principles set out in Church of Scientology of California v.
Department of Health and Social Security, [1979] 1 W.L.R.
732 (C.A.), wherein Brandon L.J. held, at p.
743: …[T]he principles applicable are, in my view, as follows: 1.

A party to litigation has a prima facie right of unrestricted inspection of the documents of which discovery has been made by the other party so far as may be necessary to dispose fairly of the case or for saving costs.
A party is not entitled to use his right of inspection for any collateral purpose.

If it is shown that there is a real risk of a party using his right for a collateral purpose, the Court has power to impose restrictions on such right in order to prevent or discourage him from doing so.

I think that this power is derived from the inherent jurisdiction of the court to prevent abuse of its process… 19 The prima face right to the unrestricted inspection of documents of which discovery has been made, and the implied undertaking not to use this right for any collateral purpose are well established.
Wachowich J. recognized that exceptions to the general rule of unrestricted inspection should be rare, at p.301: In the majority of cases, the implied undertaking is sufficient.
The next level of cases is where the Court may require a formal undertaking by the party or their Counsel not to misuse the information.
Finally, the extreme position is composed of a “small hard core of cases” where additional precautions are necessary to ensure no abuse of the discovery process… 20 In Wirth Ltd. v.
Acadia Pipe & Supply Corp.

298 (Q.B.), in considering whether there was an implied undertaking not to use information obtained through the discovery process for any purpose outside of the litigation, Lutz J. noted that a non-disclosure order may be sought where there are special circumstances.
Citing Ed Miller Sales and Church of Scientology, he suggested that the test for a non- disclosure order is that of a “real risk”.
21 Ed Miller Sales and Wirth were decided prior to the introduction of Rule 216.1 to the Alberta Rules of Court in 1996.
The relevant portions of the rule provide: 216.1
(1) The Court may modify or waive any right or power under this Part, on terms or otherwise, or may impose terms on any party, where …
(b) the expense, delay, danger or difficulty in complying fully would be grossly disproportionate to the likely benefit.
(2) Terms imposed under subrule
(1) may, without limiting the generality of subrule
(1), be made in respect of the following: …
(e) production of or access to documents, whether or not they are referred to in any pleading, particular or affidavit
(o) a confidentiality order.
22 Phoenix points out that while parties may have consented to similar orders in the past, this would be the first time a confidentiality order is approved judicially under Rule 216.1.

The introduction of Rule 216.1 in 1996 raises the question of whether it changed the test from “real risk”, as set out in Ed Miller Sales, to “grossly disproportionate danger,” which is the language used in the Rule.
The foregoing review of the jurisprudence demonstrates that the term “grossly disproportionate” was not part of the common-law test for confidentiality orders.
In certain cases, courts have spoken of “balancing,” or a “real risk.” 23 McMahon J. considered an application for a confidentiality order under Rule 216.1 in Murphy Oil Co. v.
Predator Corp., [2002] A.J.
No.
He noted, at para.
5, that Rule 216.1 codified, to a degree, the Court's inherent jurisdiction to impose restrictive conditions upon the inspection of the opposite party's records.

He went on to find, at para.16, that in the circumstances before him, the evidence did not establish “unusual circumstances or real risk of abuse.” While this suggests that McMahon J. was applying a different test from the “grossly disproportionate danger” test set out in the rule, his decision must be viewed in the context of his determination that the applicant had failed to bring evidence that would satisfy the arguably lower threshold of “real risk”, and, importantly, that the application had not been brought in a timely manner because the respondent had already produced information that it considered confidential.

In short, Murphy Oil was essentially decided on different grounds and it was not necessary to determine whether Rule 216.1 was a full codification of the Court's jurisdiction in respect of confidentiality orders.

24 There is little to be gained in questioning whether the term “grossly disproportionate” was selected because it was intended to capture existing law or, in the alternative, as an augmentation to existing standards.
Those standards were stated in variable terms in any event.

What is clear is that the legislature intended that the balance between interests be done under the rubric it selected, being “grossly disproportionate danger.” It is not open to me to rely upon the inherent jurisdiction of this Court to ignore the test set out in the Rule.
It is worth noting that in other contexts, the courts in this province have used this standard: Klapstein v.
Alberta Mortgage & Housing Corp., [1998] A.J.
No.
611 (C.A.), Gouin v.
Gouin, [2006] A.J.
No.
The pre-1996 jurisprudence remains relevant because it sets out factors to be considered and the competing values at issue.
However, the balancing of those interests must be done under the statutory requirement set out in Rule 216.1.

Application of the Rule 216.1 Test in the Context of a Confidentiality Order 25 One principle that remains unchanged from the jurisprudence prior to 1996 is that each application for a confidentiality order must be assessed on the basis of the particular circumstances, facts and evidence at hand.

The issue in every case will be whether the risk associated with disclosing the information in question is grossly disproportionate to the well recognized merits associated with full disclosure of all relevant information to the parties.
A Counsel/Expert Eyes Only Order will be the exception, and the burden is on the applicant to prove, on a balance of probabilities, all requirements of Rule 216.1.
26 The starting point is the fundamental nature of a party's right (whether plaintiff or defendant) to fully know the case against it and to instruct counsel.
At the same time, while it is true that these are important considerations, they are considerations which exist in every case.

In certain circumstances, the simple assertion of this principle may be all that is necessary to defeat the applicant's claim that disclosure of confidential or proprietary information may expose the applicant to risk grossly disproportionate to the benefit to be obtained from the disclosure.

However, when the applicant's evidence is compelling and uncontradicted, and the Court has a discretion to craft a flexible order, the evidentiary burden may shift to the respondent to demonstrate specific prejudice.

To put it another way, while the legal burden remains on the applicant to prove a grossly disproportionate danger under Rule 216.1, where the applicant has brought evidence of grossly disproportionate danger and proposes a sufficiently flexible order, it may be incumbent upon a respondent to do more than simply assert that the general principle is full disclosure.
Martin J. then noted that it was appropriate to consider the knowledge of the party to whom the disclosure was to be made, the nature of the information to be disclosed.
At pp.
336-337, she said: In Warner-Lambert Co. v.
Glaxo Laboratories Ltd., [1975] R.P.C 354, a decision of the English Court of Appeal, Buckley L.J. recognized, at pps.

360-361, that the nature of the information, and the knowledge of the parties to whom it might be disclosed in the ordinary course, are relevant considerations: Where a matter in question in an action, being that matter upon which inspection or disclosure will throw light, is of a technical nature, the party seeking discovery may well require inspection by, or disclosure to, technical and professional advisors.

If the matter be of a kind on which the party will be likely to be able with the aid of those advisers to form some kind of view of his own, it seems to me that he should normally be allowed to know as much about the facts as his advisers.

If, however, the case were one of so esoterically technical a character that even with the help of his expert advisers the party himself could really form no view of his own upon the matter in question but would be bound to act merely upon advice on the technical aspects, disclosure to him of the facts underlying the advice might serve little or no useful purpose.

In such a case a court might well be justified in directing disclosure of allegedly secret material only to expert or professional agents of the party seeking discovery on terms that they should not, without further order, pass on any information so obtained to the party himself or anyone else, but should merely advise him in the light of the information so obtained.
28 In the result, Buckley L.J. concluded that it would be appropriate to allow disclosure of proprietary information to the plaintiff.

His conclusion was based on evidence before him that the plaintiff's advisors were unable to give meaningful guidance to the plaintiff without disclosing the information, and he limited the disclosure to the “principal executive officer” of the plaintiff corporation alone.
29 The nature of the proposed order is a relevant consideration in weighing the risk of disclosure of confidential information against the benefit of full disclosure.
A carefully crafted order that preserves flexibility will reduce the negative impact of the order on the benefits associated with full disclosure to the parties.

paragraphs.text: (1) Unless the Court otherwise orders, every corporation that is a party must appoint a corporate representative. (2) Corporate representatives must (a) inform themselves of relevant and material records and relevant and material information before being questioned under this Division, (b) if questioned under this Division, bring to the questioning any records likely to be required in respect of which there is no claim of privilege, and (c) give appropriate evidence of the relevant and material records and relevant and material information. (3) The corporate representative's evidence is evidence given by the corporation. (4) On application, the Court may order corporate representatives to inform themselves of relevant and material records or relevant and material information, or both. (5) The Court may appoint a corporate representative for a party that is a corporation if the party has not done so. (6) The Court may appoint an additional or a substitute corporate representative for a party that is a corporation if (a) an appointed corporate representative is not suitable, or (b) an appointed corporate representative failed to inform himself or herself of relevant and material records and relevant and material information before being questioned.
